stages.title: Advanced linguistics and grammar
stages.hook: Why is the infinitive in 'Para eles saírem' inflected, when English and Spanish cannot do this?
explain: The personal (inflected) infinitive is a distinctive feature of Portuguese: it carries person and number endings (falar, falares, falar, falarmos, falarem). It is used when the infinitive has its own subject, different from the main clause: 'É importante eles saírem' (It is important for them to leave) or after prepositions: 'Antes de partirmos' (Before we leave). It is often optional and stylistic.

Other advanced topics: clitic placement (próclise, ênclise, mesóclise), including mesoclisis in European formal writing ('dir-lhe-ei', I will tell him); the future subjunctive, used after se, quando, assim que; and the aspectual contrast between perfect and imperfect. Variation is also grammatical: in Brazil, 'Eu vi ele' is common in speech, while formal norms prefer 'Eu o vi'.
stages.mnemonic: Different subject? The infinitive gets endings.
sentences: It is important for them to leave.
If I have time, I help.

A clitic inserted inside a future or conditional form
A noun that means a feeling
A question word used in letters
gq.why: In dir-lhe-ei the pronoun lhe sits inside the future form direi; this is called mesoclisis.

o: Partir is a noun, so the ending is needed

panel.why: The inflected infinitive marks the subject.

panel.q: Which form follows 'se' for an open future condition?
o: present indicative only: se eu tenho
panel.why: Portuguese uses the future subjunctive.

teach.model: The personal infinitive has person endings. Clitics can be proclitic, enclitic or mesoclitic. The future subjunctive follows se, quando, assim que.

stages.title: Historical development of the language
stages.hook: How did spoken Latin become Portuguese?
explain: Portuguese descends from the Vulgar Latin of the western Iberian Peninsula. It developed out of Galician-Portuguese in the Middle Ages. Typical sound changes include the loss of intervocalic l and n (Latin luna → lua), palatalisation (Latin filium → filho), nasalisation (Latin manus → mão) and the change of pl- to ch- (pluvia → chuva).

The earliest Portuguese documents date from around 1214, and medieval poets wrote lyric songs, the cantigas, in Galician-Portuguese. Later, Portuguese spread through exploration to Africa, Asia and the Americas, and contact languages produced creoles. Spelling reforms followed: 1911, 1945, and the 1990 Orthographic Agreement, implemented from 2009.
stages.mnemonic: Latin lupus, Portuguese lobo; Latin pluvia, Portuguese chuva.
sentences: The spelling agreement took effect in 2009.

gq.q: Which sound change turned pluvia into chuva?

Spelling rules for the old language
Grammar books of the sixteenth century

It is a modern dialect of Brazil
It is the common medieval ancestor of Portuguese and Galician
It is a creole of the Atlantic islands
panel.why: Both languages derive from it.

panel.q: What does the loss of intervocalic l explain?
panel.why: The l between vowels disappeared in luna.

panel.why: When Portuguese met local languages in Africa, Asia and the Americas, new contact languages developed.

teach.model: Portuguese comes from Vulgar Latin via Galician-Portuguese. Typical changes: loss of intervocalic l and n, palatalisation, nasalisation, pl- to ch-.

stages.title: Literature and cultural discourse
stages.hook: Why is 'antropofagia' a famous idea in Brazilian culture?
explain: In 1922 the Week of Modern Art in São Paulo challenged academic traditions. In 1928, Oswald de Andrade published the 'Manifesto Antropófago' (Cannibalist Manifesto), proposing that Brazilian culture should metaphorically 'devour' foreign influences and transform them into something new. Cultural discourse in the Portuguese-speaking world also debates 'lusofonia', colonial history and identity.

Postcolonial writers such as Mia Couto (Mozambique), Pepetela (Angola) and Paulina Chiziane (Mozambique) explore language, memory and power. Conceição Evaristo (Brazil) writes about Black Brazilian experience. Gilberto Freyre's idea of 'lusotropicalism' is contested by modern scholars. Present the debate fairly: different communities and critics hold different views.
stages.mnemonic: Devour, digest, make something new: antropofagia.

gq.why: Oswald de Andrade wrote it in 1928.

panel.q: What does the cannibalism metaphor mean?
o: Copying foreign culture exactly as it is
Writing only about food and eating
panel.why: It is a cultural strategy.

o: Critics argue it presents colonialism too favourably
It is about food and the kitchen
It is about music and dance
It is about spelling and accents
panel.why: Critics argue that lusotropicalism presents colonial relations too favourably, so it is treated as contested.

o: They explore language and history from new perspectives
They write dictionaries of the language
They remove the accents from words
panel.why: They explore language, memory and power from perspectives that were often missing from older literature.

teach.model: Antropofagia: absorb and transform. Postcolonial writers explore memory and power. Contested ideas such as lusotropicalism should be presented as debates.

points.ask: How do I discuss contested ideas?

stages.title: Advanced academic writing
stages.hook: What belongs in the abstract (resumo) of a Portuguese research article?
explain: An abstract (resumo) typically has about 150–250 words: context, objective, method, main results, conclusion. Typical sentences: 'Este artigo analisa ...' (This article analyses ...), 'O objetivo é ...' (The aim is ...), 'Os resultados indicam que ...' (The results indicate that ...). It is followed by 'palavras-chave' (keywords) and often an English abstract.

Style: impersonal and precise, nominalisation ('a análise de dados'), passive or impersonal se, and hedges ('sugere', 'aponta para'). References follow norms such as ABNT (Brazil) or APA/NP 405 (Portugal). Be consistent in the variety of Portuguese (Brazilian or European) throughout the text: 'utilizador' vs 'usuário', 'ficheiro' vs 'arquivo'.
stages.mnemonic: One variety, one register, from title to references.
sentences: The results indicate a clear trend.

o: Era uma vez, the start of a tale
Aliás, a marker for an aside
Varieties are identical, so mixing is harmless
Readers do not notice such differences
panel.why: Consistency shows control.

panel.q: Which pair shows a Brazil/Portugal difference?
panel.why: Different word for user.

o: It makes the text casual and spoken
It makes the text compact and abstract
It adds slang to academic writing
panel.why: Nominalisation packs actions into nouns, giving the compact abstract style of academic prose.

teach.model: A resumo states context, objective, method, results and conclusion. Use impersonal style and be consistent in variety.

stages.title: Professional translation
stages.hook: What changes when you translate a contract from Brazilian Portuguese for use in Portugal?
explain: Professional translation depends on the target audience. Vocabulary: 'contrato de locação' (Brazil) vs 'contrato de arrendamento' (Portugal); 'CPF' and 'CNPJ' (Brazilian taxpayer numbers) vs 'NIF' (Portuguese). Formal legal Portuguese uses long sentences and conventional terms such as 'partes', 'cláusula', 'foro'. Terminology must be checked against reliable sources.

Quality control: translation memory, glossaries, back-translation, peer review, and attention to numbers and dates (both varieties use the comma for decimals). Do not 'correct' the source content; flag problems to the client. Respect confidentiality. Certified translation may require a sworn translator (tradutor juramentado in Brazil).
stages.mnemonic: Know the reader and the country before choosing the word.

gq.q: Which term is the Portuguese tax number?
gq.why: NIF is the Portuguese taxpayer number, while CPF and CNPJ are Brazilian.

o: A tourist guide in a city
gq.why: In Brazil a tradutor juramentado is a sworn translator who can produce certified translations.

o: The grammar is different in the two countries

panel.why: Terms for the same legal object can differ, so the translator must know where the text will be used.

panel.why: Translating back into the source language can reveal omissions and meaning shifts.

panel.q: What should you do when the source has an error?
o: Silently change it to the correct form
Ignore it and translate as it is
Delete the sentence from the text
panel.why: The translator should report problems in the source instead of silently altering the client's text.

teach.model: Check the target audience's country, terminology, numbers and norms. Use glossaries, translation memory and back-translation. Flag source errors.

stages.title: Interpretation of complex communication
stages.hook: What does 'Vou ver' really mean when a Brazilian replies to an invitation?
explain: Complex communication often relies on implicature. 'Vou ver' (I'll see) or 'Vou tentar' (I'll try) can be a polite way of not committing. Indirectness occurs in every variety, and stereotypes such as 'Brazilians are indirect, Portuguese are direct' are only rough tendencies, so judge each speaker and situation. An interpreter must decide whether to render the implied meaning explicit or preserve the ambiguity.

Elements to track: tone, politeness markers ('por favor', 'se não for incômodo'), diminutives ('um minutinho', 'um cafezinho') that soften requests, and discourse markers. Diminutives in Portuguese often show affection or politeness, not size. Cultural references (saudade, jeitinho) should be explained briefly. Always consider speaker intention, audience and context.
stages.mnemonic: The words say less than the speaker means.
sentences: I will see if I can come.

o: A firm yes, the speaker will come
A direct question about the plan

gq.q: What does the diminutive in 'um cafezinho' often show?
o: Tiny volume only, a very small cup
Anger at the person who serves
Past tense, a cup already drunk
gq.why: In Portuguese, diminutives often express friendliness or politeness rather than small size.

o: To change the message of the speaker
To speak faster than the speaker
panel.why: Implied meaning matters.
A short explanation lets readers or listeners grasp a feeling that has no exact equivalent.

o: Intended effect depends on their culture

panel.why: The effect of a message depends on what the audience knows and expects.

teach.model: Notice implicature (vou ver), politeness, diminutives and cultural terms. Decide how explicit to be, based on intention and audience.

stages.title: Language variation and dialectology
stages.hook: Is Brazilian Portuguese closer to European Portuguese or to African varieties?
explain: Dialectology studies how language varies. Brazilian Portuguese has regional accents (carioca, paulistano, nordestino, gaúcho, caipira) and social varieties; European Portuguese has northern and central-southern varieties plus Azores and Madeira; Mirandese, a different Romance language, has had official regional recognition in Portugal since 1999. African and Asian varieties (Angola, Mozambique, Cabo Verde, Guinea-Bissau, São Tomé and Príncipe, Timor-Leste, Macau) are shaped by contact languages, and in many places Portuguese is a second language.

Features vary: gerund (estou falando) vs 'estar a + infinitive' (estou a falar); tu/você; 'nós/a gente'; variable verb agreement in popular speech. Standard varieties exist in Brazil and Portugal, and norms are developing in Africa. No variety is superior: standard forms are social conventions. Linguists describe, they do not rank, varieties.
stages.mnemonic: Describe, do not rank: every variety has rules.
sentences: Every variety has its own rules.
Portuguese is a second language for many.

gq.why: Mirandese, a Romance language of north-eastern Portugal, has had official regional recognition since 1999.

panel.why: Linguistics is descriptive.

panel.why: When Portuguese met local languages in Africa, Asia and the Americas, new contact languages developed.

teach.model: Varieties include Brazilian, European, African and Asian ones. Features: gerund vs a + infinitive, tu/você. Mirandese is a separate language. No variety is superior.

stages.title: Specialised scientific or technical language
stages.hook: How do you say 'file', 'screen' and 'user' in technical Portuguese in Lisbon and in São Paulo?
explain: Technical vocabulary differs by country. Computing: 'ficheiro' (PT) vs 'arquivo' (BR) for file; 'ecrã' (PT) vs 'tela' (BR) for screen; 'utilizador' (PT) vs 'usuário' (BR) for user; 'rato' (PT) vs 'mouse' (BR). Science: célula (cell), equação (equation), energia (energy), hipótese (hypothesis), experiência / experimento (experiment).

Style: precise, impersonal, with SI units and defined terms. Many terms are international (Greek and Latin roots), so they are close to English and Spanish. For specialised texts, use terminology databases and consult experts; avoid creating new terms where established ones exist.
stages.mnemonic: Check which country's terms your reader expects.
sentences: The file is on the screen.

panel.q: Why do technical words differ between countries?
o: Different grammar only, with the same words
panel.why: Vocabulary develops separately.

panel.q: Why can many scientific terms be understood across languages?
o: They are random, with no common source
They share Greek and Latin roots
They are English words in disguise
They are brief and easy to guess
panel.why: Many scientific terms come from Greek and Latin and are therefore similar across European languages.

panel.q: What should a translator do before coining a term?
o: Copy the word from the source text
panel.why: Use established terms.

teach.model: Terms differ between countries: ficheiro/arquivo, ecrã/tela, utilizador/usuário. Many scientific terms share Greek and Latin roots. Use established terms.

stages.title: Integrated proficiency project
stages.hook: Can you combine everything into one Portuguese project?
explain: An integrated proficiency project combines reading, listening, speaking and writing. For example: choose a Lusophone topic (a city, a writer, a music style), read two sources (one Brazilian and one European or African), listen to an interview, give a 5-minute presentation, and write a one-page report with an abstract and references. Self-assess with CEFR descriptors at B2–C1: can you argue, summarise, adapt register and handle variation?

Checklist: accurate verb forms and moods, agreement, clitic placement, consistent variety, appropriate register, clear structure and connectors, and honest use of sources. Ask a native speaker for feedback, revise, and reflect on what to practise next.
sentences: The project is about Brazilian music.

gq.q: Which skills does the project combine?
gq.why: A project combines reading, listening, speaking and writing in one purposeful task.

gq.q: Which feature shows control of variety?
gq.why: Using one variety throughout shows control, whereas mixed vocabulary looks careless.

panel.q: Why use sources from different countries?

panel.why: Sources from several countries show variety and different perspectives.

teach.model: Combine reading, listening, speaking and writing. Keep one variety, adapt register, use sources honestly, get feedback and revise.
